title: The Most Epic Revenge Stories in History
description:
A painter who put his critic in the underworld, a kidnapped Julius Caesar who kept a promise to his pirates, a noblewoman who turned privateer, a princess and her (legendary) bird trick, a nine-year-old's oath against Rome, a khan pushed too far, and the 47 ronin, plus Queen Boudica as an honorable mention: seven of history's most epic revenge stories, counted down from seven to one. We flag the legends and keep the payback off-screen. Chapters are added automatically.

#history #revenge #47ronin #juliuscaesar #historypros
youtube_title: The Most Epic Revenge Stories in History

beats.say: The Aegean Sea, 75 BC. Pirates have just kidnapped a young Roman nobleman named Julius Caesar.
Your ransom is twenty talents of silver. Pay up, Roman.
Twenty? Do you know who I am? Ask for fifty.
Yes, he asked them to raise his own ransom. That's the real story, told by the Greek writer Plutarch.
Then Caesar made the pirates a promise: one day, he'd come back and punish every one of them. They laughed.
They should not have laughed.
Today: seven of the most epic revenge stories in history. Real people, real grudges, and some very creative payback.

show.text: The Most Epic Revenge Stories in History

beats.say: Number seven: Michelangelo, one of the most famous artists of Renaissance Italy.
For about five years, he painted a giant wall in the Pope's own chapel. It's called The Last Judgment.
But one man hated it: Biagio da Cesena, the Pope's master of ceremonies. Basically, the man in charge of church events.
He complained that the painting was full of naked people, and said it belonged in a bathhouse, not a chapel.
This belongs in a tavern, not a holy chapel!
Noted.
So Michelangelo painted Biagio into the picture, as Minos, a judge of the underworld, complete with donkey ears.
Biagio ran to Pope Paul the Third to complain. The story goes that the Pope joked that he had no power over hell, so the portrait had to stay.
And it's still there, in the corner of the Sistine Chapel. Millions of tourists see Biagio's donkey ears every year.
Number six: back to Julius Caesar and those pirates.
Caesar was sailing to Rhodes, a Greek island, to study public speaking. Pirates grabbed him near a tiny island called Pharmacusa.
His friends went off to collect fifty talents of silver. That took thirty-eight days.

show.label: Days Caesar spent as a hostage
show.sub: while his friends collected 50 talents of silver

beats.say: Caesar didn't act like a prisoner. He told the pirates to keep quiet while he slept. He wrote poems and read them out loud.
If they didn't clap, he called them uneducated barbarians, right to their faces.
Ha! This kid is hilarious.
I'm serious. I'll be back for all of you.
The ransom arrived and Caesar was freed. He went straight to the city of Miletus, gathered ships, and sailed right back.
He caught the pirates still at their island, and took the silver back too.
Then he had them executed, exactly as he'd promised. They thought he was joking. He wasn't.
Number five: Jeanne de Clisson, a rich noblewoman from Brittany, in western France.
In 1343, France and England were at war. The King of France, Philip the Sixth, accused Jeanne's husband, Olivier, of secretly helping the English.
Olivier was executed for treason. Jeanne was heartbroken, then furious. She wanted the king to pay.
So she sold her lands and jewels, and bought warships.
Tell the King of France I'm coming for his ships.
Later tales add the best details: ships painted black, blood-red sails, and a flagship called My Revenge.
Records confirm France branded her a traitor, and England's king backed her. Accounts say she raided French ships and coasts for years.
People called her the Lioness of Brittany. And the irony? Her son grew up to command the entire French army.
Number four comes with a warning label: it's partly legend.
It comes from the Primary Chronicle, a history written in Kyiv more than a century and a half after it happened.
In 945, Prince Igor of Kyiv went to collect taxes from a forest tribe called the Drevlians. Then he came back for more. So the Drevlians killed him.
His widow, Princess Olga, now ruled for their little son.
The Drevlians sent messengers with an offer: marry our prince.
How lovely. Do come in.
According to the Chronicle, every welcome was a trap: a fake honor, a fake bath, a fake funeral feast. The Drevlians fell for all of them.
Next, Olga's army surrounded their main town, Iskorosten. After a long siege, she offered peace for a tiny price.
Just three pigeons and three sparrows from every house.
The townspeople happily paid. Olga's soldiers tied burning material to the birds, and let them go.
The birds flew home to their nests, under the straw roofs, and the whole town caught fire at once.
And the twist? Olga later became a Christian, and today she's a saint.
Number three: Hannibal of Carthage, a rich city in North Africa, and Rome's great rival.
Carthage had just lost a long war to Rome. Hannibal's father, the general Hamilcar, never forgave them.
In 237 BC, Hamilcar was about to lead an army to Spain. His nine-year-old son begged to come along.
You can come. But first, put your hand on the sacrifice, and swear.
I swear!
Decades later, Hannibal told this story to a foreign king, and the Greek historian Polybius wrote it down.
In Hannibal's own words, he had to swear that he would never be friends with Rome.

show.text: …and swear that I would never be friends with Rome.
show.who: Hannibal, as recorded by Polybius, Histories, Book 3

beats.say: And he kept that promise. In 218 BC, Hannibal marched an army from Spain, over the Alps, into Italy.
He brought war elephants. Around thirty-seven of them. Over the mountains.

show.label: War elephants Hannibal led toward the Alps
show.sub: most died within a few months

beats.say: Rome did not see that coming.
In 216 BC, at Cannae in southern Italy, he crushed a much bigger Roman army. Military schools still study that battle today.
He never captured Rome itself. But for about fifteen years, he was Rome's worst nightmare. Oath kept.
Number two: Genghis Khan, the founder of the Mongol Empire.
In 1218, he wanted to trade with his rich neighbor, the Khwarazmian Empire, a huge Muslim empire in Central Asia.
So he sent a big trade caravan, loaded with gold and silk.
At the border town of Otrar, the governor, Inalchuq, called the merchants spies, and had them killed.
About four hundred and fifty men, gone.

show.label: People in Genghis Khan's trade caravan

beats.say: Fine. Let's try talking first.
He sent envoys to the Shah, the emperor, asking him to hand the governor over.
The Shah had one envoy killed, and the others' beards shaved off. That was a massive insult.
Wrong answer.
In 1219, the Mongols invaded. Over the next year, Otrar fell, then the great cities of Bukhara and Samarkand.
The Shah fled west, with Mongol riders chasing him across Iran. In 1220, he died on a tiny island in the Caspian Sea.
Within about two years, a huge empire was gone. Huge numbers of ordinary people died too, which is the dark side of this story.
And number one: the forty-seven ronin of Japan.
In 1701, at the shogun's castle in Edo, today's Tokyo, a young lord named Asano lost his temper with a top official named Kira.
Kira taught court manners. The usual story is that he'd been insulting Asano for weeks. Asano drew his sword and wounded him.
Drawing a sword in the shogun's castle was a serious crime. Asano was sentenced to die that same day. Kira wasn't punished at all.
Asano's samurai lost their master, their jobs, and their home. Now they were ronin: samurai with no master.
Their leader, Ōishi Kuranosuke, had a plan. Step one: look like a total mess.
Popular accounts say he partied in public near Kyoto, so Kira's spies would think he'd given up.
Sir, people say you've forgotten our master.
Good. Let them say it.
For almost two years, they waited. Then, on a snowy night in early 1703, forty-seven of them broke into Kira's house in Edo.
They found Kira hiding, and took their revenge for their master.
At dawn, they marched across the city to their master's grave at Sengaku-ji temple, to tell him it was done. Then they turned themselves in.
The government had a problem. They'd broken the law, but everyone admired their loyalty. In the end, forty-six were ordered to die by seppuku, the samurai's ritual death.
They were buried next to their master. More than three hundred years later, people still leave incense at their graves.
Almost two years of patience, one night of payback, and a story Japan has retold in plays and movies ever since.
Honorable mention: Boudica, queen of the Iceni, a tribe in eastern Britain.
When her husband died, Roman officials seized the family's lands, and mistreated Boudica and her daughters. That's according to the Roman historian Tacitus.
So she raised a huge army and burned three Roman towns, including Londinium, which we now call London.
Rome finally beat her. But today, a bronze statue of Boudica in her war chariot stands right beside Parliament in London.
So that's the list: a painted insult, a kidnapped poet, a pirate lioness, a bird trick, a lifelong oath, a furious khan, and forty-seven patient samurai.
Which revenge was the most epic? Tell us in the comments.
